According to a recent report in the U.S. News and World Report, the Soviet Union is now flying arms to Nicaragua not only through Cuba but also directly through Newfoundland. speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. It deals with the fact that three more partners have withdrawn from the Alsands consortium, putting that project in serious jeopardy. What is the minister doing about it?

subsubtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF PARTNERS IN ALSANDS PROJECT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, last night I had a meeting in Toronto with senior officers of Shell Canada, and today officials of the government of Alberta and the Government of Canada are meeting with officials and technicians representing the companies concerned. speechtext:

The National Energy program will spur oil sands development. The positive impact of the program on oil sands development can be illustrated by its effect on the commercial viability of the Alsands project-

Oral Questions
We now know that that statement is about as accurate as other statements the minister has made. Would the minister tell the House what changes he will make in the National Energy Program to ensure that at least this project goes ahead?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Madam Speaker, with respect to the National Energy Program I draw to the hon. member's attention the fact that there has been an agreement with Alberta which provides that we pay the international price for oil from the tar sands.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: My very knowledgeable friend who was the former minister of finance and who is a great specialist on taxes on oil and gas says, "So what". Does he suggest that we should ask the taxpayers and the consumers of Canada to pay more than world price for tar sands oil? That is not the view of this government. This government has taken the view that we should pay the world price or the international price for oil from those projects. Bunk.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT INTEREST RATE POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Yesterday in his speech in New York he said that the government had rejected all pleas to embark on a course of economic stimulation, and indicated that the government was quite prepared to sit back and wait for the recovery of the United States economy. At the same time the Prime Minister was standing up in this house telling us that the government was considering the possibility of lowering interest rates to provide stimulus to the economy.
Now that the minister is under pressure from the people of Canada, the ten provincial premiers, members of his own caucus and even the Prime Minister, is he prepared to abandon his disastrous high interest rate policy, or will he continue to refuse to take any independent action that would allow the country to lead its own economic recovery?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT INTEREST RATE POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is true that I stated in New York yesterday that I did not see the solution to our problems to be spending our way out of the recession, and add to the deficit and add to the inflationary pressures in the economy. That is my view, and it is the policy that has been endorsed on three separate occasions in the House since the budget was presented.
I want to tell the hon. member that the comment which I made yesterday, to the effect that we are opposed to the suggestion that interest rates can be forced down significantly if only we accept the depreciation in the value of our dollar, is a statement of our policy. It is a policy that is not at all altered

or changed by any comments made yesterday in the House by the Prime Minister.

DEFICIT IN TRADE IN MANUFACTURED GOODS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, that will not be welcome news to the millions of Canadians who are unemployed and the small businesses that are going bankrupt.
The minister also stated in New York yesterday that he would resist any pressure to protect this country's manufacturing industries. How can he continue to advocate that Canada remain the international boy scout of free trade when we racked up a $21 billion trade deficit in manufactured goods last year and lost over 300,000 jobs in total, in this vital sector of our economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: DEFICIT IN TRADE IN MANUFACTURED GOODS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, what 1 said yesterday is that it is not our intention to join in a policy of increased protectionism at the present time. That is a very strong temptation in every country-to put up trade barriers and adopt "beggar-thy-neighbour" policies. We know from past experience that that would be very dangerous to Canada because we depend on a very dynamic international trading system. If we did anything to impair that, we would be putting ourselves at a very grave disadvantage.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the position in the New Democratic Party is that, if they want profits, it is necessary for companies to provide Canadians with paycheques as well. Although the government continues to restate its concern for the unemployed in Canada, the weakness of its commitment became clearer than ever earlier this week when the estimates came before the House. In the face of over a million people unemployed, the government actually cut $102 million from its already meagre job-creation budget. On the one hand, how can the government keep telling the unemployed of Canada that it recognizes and is greatly concerned about their plight, but on the other hand callously cut 35 per cent from this portion of the budget?

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: SINKING OF "OCEAN RANGER"-LACK OF RESCUE CRAFT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am told that 1 can only ask one question. Perhaps because of the importance of it you will let me put it in two parts. My question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. Would the minister tell the House why in the early hours of February 15, the critical hours, there were no fixed wing aircraft on the ground or no surface vessels in the area of the sinking of the Ocean Ranger, and what rescue operations there were, were not being directed by the Air-Sea Rescue Centre in Halifax but by the Mobil Oil company?
Could the minister also tell the house how he could find $22 million for two executive aircraft but could not find money to instal weather radar in the rescue helicopters in Gander?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: SINKING OF "OCEAN RANGER"-LACK OF RESCUE CRAFT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I understand very well the concerns of the hon. member for St. John's East about the Ocean Ranger incident. I can assure him that I share his concern about what happened in this case. First of all, I do not think any orders were given by any of Mobil's people to the rescue centre. The co-ordination centre in Halifax is the lead centre and it gives whatever orders must be given concerning search and rescue. As far as improvements in Newfoundland in search and rescue capabilities are concerned, I can send to the hon. member a list of what we have done since 1976. We have stationed three helicopters in Gander and two ocean vessels since then. I think we have improved tremendously the effectiveness of search and rescue operations in the area.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION IN UNITED STATES CONGRESS

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION IN UNITED STATES CONGRESS
speechtext:
Madam speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. First 1 would like to congratulate the government for its belated recognition of its responsibilities. I think it has announced a joint inquiry into the terrible Ocean Ranger disaster with the province of Newfoundland. I hope this six-member commission will do the job of thoroughly exploring the issue. It now realizes that no ultimatum was given by the province of Newfoundland, and it has co-operated with them in this endeavour.
In Washington today, the Congressional merchant marine subcommittee headed by Mr. Biaggi is examining a bill to remove the right of non-American workers on United States-owned oil drilling rigs or vessels to recover damages from U.S. companies in U.S. courts for injuries suffered outside U.S. waters. The legislation will not be retroactive, but it is very important in view of the fact that the Ocean Ranger was a U.S.-owned rig operating outside U.S. waters. Has the government appointed representatives to appear before the committee to oppose the passage of the bill or to make representations on behalf of Canadian citizens and the Canadian government? If
so, who are they and what are their instructions? Will we do everything we can to see that that legislation is not passed by the United States Congress?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION IN UNITED STATES CONGRESS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, indeed we are well aware of the bill of Representative Biaggi. It was introduced on October 29, and therefore was not introduced in contemplation of this accident. It would not have the effect of barring completely law suits by aliens in United States courts, but it would make them seek remedies in other courts first before it would allow them to have recourse to United States courts. Of course we are watching it very closely, and there is some uncertainty as to legislative jurisdiction over semi-submersible rigs, depending upon whether they are to be classified in international law as ships of a country or as projections of a coastal state.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF GAS PIPELINE TO MARITIME PROVINCES

Obviously we cannot have a reasonable debate as to the propriety of the form until we have the bill. We do not have the bill until it is given first reading and is printed. Therefore, we have a Catch-22 situation. Mr. Speaker Lamoureux dealt with this on January 26, 1971, when he said:
Business of the House
In my view it should be the responsibility of the Chair, when such bill is introduced and given first reading, to take the initiative and raise the matter for the consideration of the House by way of a point of order-
My suggestion to the Chair is that the Chair permit a caveat on first reading to allow us the opportunity over the weekend to examine this bill to find out if in fact our concerns are legitimate, and on Monday, if it is deemed desirable, to discuss whether the bill is in order or not, allowing the opportunity for the Chair to exercise its discretion in a way that is not prejudiced by the fact that we will have completed first reading.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-89 ON SECOND READING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it was three months ago almost to the day that I first asked for the support of all members of the House to consider the urgency of the measures in Bill C-89. The last two paragraphes of my comments on that day were as follows:
The task now. Madam Speaker, is for the House to translate into action its expressed concern for housing matters and Canadians thereby affected. I will soon table a bill to amend the National Housing Act. This legislation is important. It will enable the government to assist households renewing their mortgage; it will enable the government to assist first-time home buyers through modifications to the mortgage instrument; and it will enable additional stimulus to be provided to rental production by allowing CMHC to insure higher loan amounts on rental production.
I trust and pray. Madam Speaker, that just as my confidence in the government was vindicated by the budget, so too will my confidence in the good sense of the hon. members of the House be vindicated by their speedy passage of the housing legislation so sorely needed by many Canadians today.
I wish that confidence had been borne out.
In April of 1980 the Speech from the Throne set the basis- and should have alerted this House-to the general intentions of the government with respect to housing. The Speech from the Throne stated that the government would:
-act to assist those unable to bear the burden of renegotiating their home mortgages in the present abnormal situation so that the spectre of foreclosure will be avoided.
We described how this would be approached by the government. We were convinced that the government could do this:
-without the government embarking upon a major subsidy program.
Those signals were sent to the opposition many, many months ago. The Canada mortgage renewal plan introduced in the budget on November 12 did just that. It followed the intentions of the government I have laid out. It is a plan to assist Canadians who are unable to help themselves with guarantees, through interest deferral or grants up to $3,000 per household.
This legislation was tabled in this House prior to December. I had copies of the draft legislation hand delivered to the housing critics of the opposition parties. In January prior to the return of this House to its normal business I sought the cooperation of the parties through their respective spokesmen- in the case of the New Democratic Party, spokeswoman.
We have been discussing this legislation now for five days. What is particularly perturbing to me-and a disappointment-is the fact that hon. members opposite asked in October and November that I or my office use what influence we
had to assist Canadians who were troubled about mortgage renewals. I received nearly 400 requests for assistance from hon. members opposite. This legislation is required in order that I can indeed assist not only hon. members opposite but also the many Canadians who have sought the assistance provided in the programs in Bill C-89.
In addition to that, when hon. members opposite returned in the fall, they tabled many petitions containing thousands of signatures of concerned Canadians. I personally signed responses to over 10,000 Canadians advising that the government would take action and that it would be in accordance with the principles I have enunciated in these brief remarks. This legislation is required to assist many of those Canadians.
I would like to stress that the commitment of the budget was $350 million over the next two years to encourage the construction of rental accommodation. One third of those units promoted by that budgetary commitment are what we refer to as rent-geared-to-income accommodation. Any hon. member who has any experience in the housing field knows that that program through the years in most of the provinces of Canada has been one of the most effective ways of providing affordable accommodation to Canadians at lower income levels. The delivery of that accommodation to Canadians is being delayed by the delay of this legislation. Without this legislation we cannot proceed with that program.
There has been the complaint that this bill is not enough, but I point out, as I did to the new critic for the New Democratic Party, that the 15,000 units are a minimum and that after we receive proposals and responses from the building community the $350 million could result in many thousands of additional units over and above the 15,000. The many jobs which will be created through the construction of that rental accommodation will be the result of this legislation.
Hon. members have recounted in this House the experience in their communities, and they have asked for government programs. That was done today by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie). Hon. members have been seeking government programs to create employment across the country. The legislation before us, Bill C-89, for which we have sought co-operation, is one of the tools which addresses that problem. There is a potential of 70,000 person years generated through the expenditure of $350 million. I felt that would have motivated more support and a speedier response to the legislation and possibly would have obviated the necessity of the government's proposing the motion I am proposing today.
In conclusion, I remind hon. members that the blueprint for action of this government in the Speech from the Throne in April, 1980, addressed not only the needs of those in this country who need help most and the intentions of the government to respond in a real way to those who need help most, but it also addressed the posture of the government in terms of how it goes about general government business. One of the principles is a recognition that Canadians do not necessarily want more government. They want more effective government.
February 25, 1982

The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation is dealt with in Bill C-89. From comments of hon. members on both sides of this House and from personal representations made by hon. members, I know that the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation has served Canadians and the representatives of Canadians well over the last few years. The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation needs this legislation to make its operation more effective in the handling of claims, in the area of underwriting and in being able to support the lending institutions with the types of new mortgage documents which are now generated in our changing economic climate. Those provisions have not been attacked. In five days of debate not a single word of criticism has been addressed to those objectives.
1 will conclude by saying that 1 wish we had the support of hon. members opposite. I believe that the response of the government in this bill is a sensible and sensitive one to a difficult problem.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just witnessed what I consider to be one of the most outstanding examples of hypocrisy that I have seen around here in a long time. The minister who is responsible for housing pleads with us; he tells us how he tried to cajole us into getting on with the bill and then damns himself out of his own mouth. The very man who stands in his place today to bring in a closure motion talks about the business of Bill C-89 being incorporated in the Speech from the Throne in April 1980!
So much for urgency, Mr. Speaker. It did not see the light of day again until the budget of November 12, 1981. Again, so much for urgency, so much for discharging a promise to the home owners of this country in the budget of April 1980. The bill does not come before the House for second reading until February 8, 1982, three full months after the introduction of the budget. And still the minister talks about urgency.
Let us look at the record of debate on Bill C-89 since second reading debate commenced on February 8, 1982. Debate was continued on February 9, then was interrupted on February 10 because the government wanted to deal with Bill C-90, the Customs Tariff bill. It was picked up again on February 11 and then we did not get back to it until February 22.
What happened during the intervening days? There was an allotted day. The government could have set that aside; it manages the business of the House so it could have said that it wanted to get on with Bill C-89 because it was a matter of urgency. Apart from an allotted day, we had the labour benefits bill, the Canagrex bill, the taxation and borrowing authority bill, a supply day, the labour benefits bill again- everything but Bill C-89. Yet the minister has the unmitigated gall to stand in his place and say that the House has dragged its feet and that this bill is a matter of urgency. We have had five days to deal with this bill. That is the only opportunity we will have to examine the housing crisis and the government's response to it.
Time Allocation
It is worth looking at the record of those five days, Mr. Speaker. It is not only members of the opposition that have been carrying the debate; members of the government party have participated, as have members of the NDP. It was only when the minister felt that the debate was going on a little bit too long that he decided to pull his members back. But that is no reason for us to withdraw and not discharge our responsibilities to the people in this country.
There is not a member sitting in this House who is not faced with a critical housing crisis in his or her constituency.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-89 ON SECOND READING
speechtext: Nonsense!

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER BILL C-89 ON SECOND READING
speechtext:
Yet the government has the unmitigated gall to invoke closure after five days of debate-to invoke closure on a bill that will probably pass second reading with a nod. No one is opposed to the principle of the bill. What we have said in speech after speech after speech is that the bill offers a mere pittance; it does not go far enough; it does not significantly address the problems of home owners nor the acute shortage of rental accommodation in this country. But because of the pittance it provides for those in dire straits, no one in this House is going to vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, we have heard criticism levelled at the opposition today that we are mindless obstructionists, that we are filibustering this and other bills and that we are not co-operating with the government.
I would first like to point out that this is another closure debate. That is precisely what it is. Whether it is under Standing Order 75 or 33, it cuts off, or limits, debate. I would like to give a few figures from this session of Parliament to demonstrate that the opposition has taken its responsibility seriously. We have co-operated with the government when that co-operation was due.
In looking through the figures, I find that 84 bills have been given first, second and third reading in this single session of Parliament. In addition, 1 1 other bills have gone through first and second reading and some have gone as far as report stage. Others have been dealt with seriously in various committees.
The record shows that we on this side of the House have done our best to ensure that good legislation is passed when it is put forward by the government and passed as quickly as is reasonable and commensurate with a reasonable amount of debate on the subject.
I do not think on this or any other occasion in this session of Parliament have we acted irresponsibly or engaged in what members opposite so flippantly call filibusters. It is true on occasion Parliament has dug in its heels. For example, Bill C-48 would radically change the whole approach to oil and gas legislation in much of Canada. We did not like that. History will prove that was a bad law for Canada. In that instance we were fully justified in digging in our heels.
Had the government been prepared to show that it was willing to make some deals with regard to what other members in this House wanted and had it backed off a little, it would have had our co-operation on the oil and gas legislation, but that was not to be the case. The government wanted to ram it through at all costs.
Hon. members will notice that Standing Order 75C has been used in a number of instances, particularly on Bill C-48. Standing Order 33 has been used on a couple of occasions. I am becoming very concerned. In the past, closure was looked upon as something out of the ordinary. It only occurred when there was a real impasse. Governments were reluctant to use it. They respected the right of Members of Parliament to debate matters and hopefully arrive at sensible compromises. That is not the case with this government which uses closure as a matter of course. When the government now uses closure, members of this House and the public are not so abashed. It is like crying wolf. The first time a lot of people get upset and rush about. After it has been done 12, 13, 14 or 15 times, people get used to it. I am concerned that the people of Canada are becoming used to the government-imposed closure. I
February 25, 1982

think that this continual use of closure constitutes an abuse of Parliament.
As Members of Parliament we have to consider what we should be doing. Surely it is our function to engage in public debate on the major issues of the day. We are paid to consider these problems and to pose possible solutions to them. We are paid to engage in debate so that Canadians can follow that debate and present their views through us on a particular subject. The issue today is housing and it is a matter of great concern throughout the country. I, as well as many other members I am sure, have received a considerable amount of mail on this subject, not to mention telephone calls.
Particular issues on housing may differ from one area of Canada to another, as was illustrated by the hon. member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons) who just spoke. He expressed his views on how this bill would solve housing problems in one area of Newfoundland. I am not familiar with that part of Newfoundland and this bill may, indeed, help that area. I doubt it, but I can tell him that it will not solve the fundamental housing problem in my part of Canada.
In my part of Canada we are faced with the high mortgage interest rates which are uniform across Canada, and in addition we are faced with extremely high utility expenses. For instance, the electrical bill for an average home in my town, not including electricity to heat the home but just for basic uses such as lighting, fridge and stove, is approximately $250 per month. During the cold winter months when you must pay $1.50 per gallon for heating oil, since there is no gas in my area, the heating bill for the average house is approximately $350 per month. When you add the utilities and the heating costs together, it comes to more than $700 per month. This expense when added to mortgage costs makes it especially difficult for people to own their homes.
I have found this debate on the housing question interesting and useful. I have learned a number of things. I have discovered that the general approach taken by the three parties in the House is quite different. The approach of the government is to do very little. It is apparently satisfied with those policies which are in place. It proposes only to make a few technical changes and a few minor amendments.

The main point I wish to make on this debate on closure is that I strongly take exception to the fact that the government uses closure as a matter of course. It will not allow policy and legislation to be developed in the House. Legislation has been developed within the public service, brought forward and Parliament is asked to rubber-stamp it. I, for one, believe that one of the most significant aspects about which Parliament must now legislate has to do with the fact that, in our opinion, all sectors must get involved if we are to set the current situation on a more constructive course. It seems to us, Mr. Speaker, that our very first responsibility is to lend a hand to Canadian individuals and families that may be putting their house on the line because of the soaring interest rates they have to cope with when they renew their mortgage. Secondly, through the Canadian rental housing construction plan, the government calls upon private enterprise so that together we can face the challenge of providing rental accommodation in those regions where there is practically none. At the same time, we have proposed measures that will enable the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to operate more effectively, by giving greater flexibility to operations relating to the insurance regulations already provided under the act, measures which from now on will authorize the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to adjust premiums according to the risk involved.
This aspect of the amendments indicates once again that the government is very receptive to contributions from all sides and is in favour of team work. I wish I could say the same about the cooperation shown by some members of the opposition. Although we have observed that in some ways they are supportive of this important bill, it has now been three weeks since the bill was tabled in the House. They have wasted two weeks instead of acting right away to provide immediate assistance to Canadians across the country who need it most. We on the government side are convinced that it is very important Canadians should receive assistance through the Canada mortgage renewal plan, the Canada rental assistance plan and other amendments to the National Housing Act and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, all of which will help the corporation to meet requests for assistance more positively and to operate more effectively on the market in question. Mr. Speaker, that is why we feel that we must get on with this business instead of wasting precious time on useless verbiage. It is time to act. Whatever our politics may
be, to all Canadians who today are waiting for federal housing assistance, actions speak louder than words. So, let us stop this empty chatter, let us stop indulging in petty politics to make the leader opposite look good. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if this is not another string of filibusters! Well, Mr. Speaker, here we go again. Any time the government senses that we in the official opposition are getting our message across to the public and any time it senses we are getting a little too close to the bone and exposing the weaknesses of its policies, zap! Down comes the guillotine. It is not unusual for this government, however, to cut off freedom of speech, freedom of expression and the right of individuals to express what they wish against government policies, whether inside or outside this Parliament.
This government seems to be gathering momentum these past 48 hours, and the cutting off of free speech has now become a rather ominous hallmark of this government. That applies to individual public servants who, in their free time, see fit to criticize government policies which deserve criticizing, and it certainly seems to apply to Members of Parliament who are duly elected to speak on behalf of their constituents and on behalf of the people of Canada in this Parliament. We can be cut off just as quickly.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith) attempts to split hairs and draw a distinction between Standing Order 33 and Standing Order 75C by suggesting there is a difference between time allocation and closure. With respect, Sir, the parliamentary secretary is a horse's foot if he thinks the public or we in the opposition are going to believe that. It is closure. Standing Order 75C or time allocation: closure is closure by any other name or any other number the government chooses to apply to it.
Closure has been used eight times-this will be the ninth- in the last year and a half. In July, 1980, closure was used on the pipeline debate for the summer recess. On December 4, 1981 closure was used at the third reading stage of Bill C-48, the Canada Oil and Gas Act. On June 8, 1981, closure was used at the third reading stage of Bill C-57, to amend the Excise Tax Act. On March 31, 1981, closure was used at the report stage of Bill C-59, borrowing authority. On February 12, 1981, closure was used at the second reading stage of Bill C-59, borrowing authority. On January 13, 1981, closure was used at the second reading stage of Bill C-48, the Canada Oil and Gas Act. On June 9, 1981, closure was used at the second reading stage of Bill C-30, borrowing authority. Today, February, 25, 1982, closure is being used at the second reading stage of Bill C-89, an extremely important piece of legislation.
February 25, 1982

When I first saw Parliament in action, it was engaged in an extremely emotional debate on closure arising from the pipeline debate of 1956. As 1 understood it, closure was only used when there was a flagrant abuse of the time of the House, and the onus was then on the government to prove, when it brought in closure, that there had been abuse of the time of the House. Nobody on the government side could possibly prove that there has been a flagrant abuse of the time of this House of Commons after five days of discussing one of the most critical issues facing Canada today and one of the most important pieces of legislation which has come before us, amendments to the National Housing Act.
There is absolutely no question that the subject uppermost in the minds of Canadians these days is housing. Uppermost in their minds as well are mortgage renewals. Not only are Canadians faced-indeed, crippled-with a housing crisis which has been exacerbated by high interest rates, but also know, because of my responsibilities as consumer and corporate affairs critic looking into the issue of hazardous products, about the nightmare people are facing in relation to urea formaldehyde foam insulation, a form of insulation which is hurting people. It is doing damage to people. This situation was manufactured by this government, encouraged by this government and promoted by this government. People were paid by this government to put UFF1 into their homes. Then this government began to worry, temporarily banned and then permanently banned UFF1, and it is now doing its best to duck its ultimate responsibility for this monstrous blunder.
That is only one aspect of the terrible housing crisis facing the people of Canada. The plight of those victims must be addressed and, in light of the United States ban on UFFI this week, it becomes even more acute.
Let me get back to the procedural aspect of this and why we feel it is so important that we must have the maximum opportunity to discuss this housing legislation. The reason the government says it must bring down the guillotine and cut off debate is that this matter has to go to committee. The fact is that there are no other housing bills on the table. We want to discuss the entire housing situation, and the government is not yet ready for committee. It has not yet made witnesses ready, but the House of Commons has the attention of the nation as we discuss the critical housing situation before us.
The problem with committee is that once we get there we are frustrated to the extreme because bills of tremendous importance are automatically given "yeas" by the majority members of the parliamentary committee, according to the instructions given to them by their superiors. In my view, committees can be a sham under a majority Liberal government.

As one hon. member said, once we get this bill through the committee and through third and final reading here-over the senseless, mindless opposition- then we can get on with the government's tinkering with the National Housing Act. Is it not too bad that there is an opposition here and that it is not just a one-party system in this country? That is the way these fellows would like to operate. It is too bad there is an opposition which can raise serious concerns on behalf of the people of Canada in terms of very meaningful and serious legislation and serious amendments we want to propose. They have their own internal operation. Anyone who thinks we can get fundamental amendments through committee, let alone through third reading stage, does not know how Parliament works under a majority Liberal government. When we reach the third reading stage then, of course, the government will probably bring in another closure motion.
The Liberal government may see fit to lower the boom on our ability to discuss this and other legislation. It can and will lower the boom in any way it sees fit; but I warn this government that the people of Canada will lower the boom on it in the interests of the preservation of free speech in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I will not have been a member of Parliament for three years until next May, but already 1 have lived through a number of debates about closure or time allocation. I want to preface my remarks today by saying that one might feel more well disposed to the need of the government for time allocation if one had the feeling that the issue of parliamentary reform had priority and was on the front burner rather than on the back burner of the government's schedule. I think all hon. members would acknowledge the need for some measure of improvement in the way we deal with matters in the House so that the opposition is not constantly put in the position of having to respond to moves like this by the government.
I think the real reason the government wants to put an end to debate on the measure to deal with the problem of people losing their homes as a result of its high interest policy is that it does not want to discuss the incredibly desperate situation that many Canadians find themselves in as a result of its policies in the public eye any longer.
My basic objection to the bill is, first of all, that it came before us so late. We heard in the throne speech in 1980, two years ago, that the Liberals were going to do something for people who were affected by high interest rates. Now we have the hypocrisy of the minister's blaming the delay on the opposition when we have only debated this bill for five days.
The reason for the motion is that the government does not want to hear about the plight of the Canadian people. I think it feels guilty about the abysmal inadequacy of the bill, which only postpones the day of reckoning for many people. Instead of doing something about high interest rates and the monopoly power of the banks over the Canadian economy, all it has done is to subsidize the banks. It has done nothing for the home owner who finds himself in a desperate situation.
The hon. member who just spoke mentioned the problems that some people have experienced with urea formaldehyde foam insulation. Mr. Speaker, one of my constituents is under attack by the government on three fronts. First of all, his mortgage is about to be renewed and, as a result, his payments will double. He is a young family man and that would be difficult enough, but his second problem, as a result of high interest rates and the downturn of the economy is that his
employer, Canadian National Railways, has laid him off. CN says there has been a downturn in its revenues. Mr. Speaker, he has been laid off by a Crown corporation which made a profit last year and therefore should be employing more people. His third problem is that he has urea formaldehyde foam insulation in his house. He cannot renew his mortgage, he cannot sell his house and he cannot work. That is the situation in which this particular Canadian has been put by the government.
We are not just talking about some abstract economic instrument that in their wisdom the experts have been forced to use, when we talk about high interest rates, Mr. Speaker. We are talking about a basic decision that has been made by people. God only knows where. I cannot figure out where some of these decisions originate. Some people say they come from Washington, some say they come from the Trilateral Commission and some say they come from the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), but I suspect he is but a little cog in a very big wheel. Wherever it was made, the decision was that the problems of the western industrialized economies would be fought on the backs of people who do not have the power to protect themselves against high interest rates. That is an immoral, political decision.
Much of the debate in this House ignores the reality that high interest rates are not something which in general cause the powerful to suffer; it is the people who cannot wait for the end of what may turn out to be a longer recession than the Minister of Finance has in mind who are hurt by the policies of the government, or by the acquiesence of the government to policies which are set somewhere else. In either case, the decision is shameful.
The problem of high interest rates points to one of the fundamental absurdities of our economic system. The people who always talk about productivity are the same people who are now putting all their money into non-productive places. They are productive places in so far as they make money, but not in so far as they build houses, create jobs and produce the necessities of life. I think interest rates are the best example of the absurdity of the present economic doctrine under which we live. I hope the people of Canada will take the opportunity presented by the high interest rate crisis to see how contradictory and inhuman the system is.
The Liberals want to bring this debate to an end so that there is no opportunity for reflection by the Canadian people, in so far as that can be stimulated by Members of Parliament speaking on their behalf. It is in the interests of the government to stifle that kind of reflection. Its back is to the wall and it does not know what to do. It has offered a pittance to people in dire straits. All it has done is to defer the evil day by refusing to face up to the basic economic problems in the Canadian economy.

COMMUNICATIONS BETWEEN GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCEOF SASKATCHEWAN CONCERNING RESIDENTIAL MORTGAGES AND HOME FORECLOSURES
speechtext:
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House copies of all communications during 1981 between the government and/or the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the government of the province of Saskatchewan dealing with residential mortgages and home foreclosures.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is appropriate that we are able to debate this motion today in the middle of the ongoing debate on Bill C-89. It is particularly appropriate because it will give us the opportunity to discuss another aspect of housing-the difficulties created by the simple fact that the physical aspects of construction, in the literal sense, are a provincial responsibility. Provincial governments by their powers are able not only to intervene in the housing field, but they have a responsibility which is certainly not less than the responsibility of the federal government.
The motion refers specifically to correspondence between the federal government and the government of the province of Saskatchewan. When there is communication or correspondence, the normal procedure is for the federal government to request permission of the provincial government for the documents to be released. It is my understanding that this permission has been requested. It is possible in due course that the Saskatchewan government will give approval for the release of these documents. I take issue with the tendency of the two levels of government to communicate with each other in this fashion, because I believe all such communications should be open and available to the public so that the public at large can see precisely what each level of government is
Housing
attempting to do, particularly in a field where there is some conflict of jurisdiction.
The Saskatchewan home owners protection act became law on December 11, 1981. It affords protection to home owners against loss of their principal residences from January 1, 1982, to December 31, 1982. Of course, this has concerned the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation because of its interest in mortgages which it insures and the possibility that there could be some additional costs incurred by the Crown corporation as a result of the provincial legislation. After some two months of operation two legal tests were conducted in Saskatchewan, and there was no clear impression left in anyone's mind as to exactly how it will operate for the rest of the year. Neither of the cases heard set any standard to determine who is to be protected under the law, and at the moment one of the two cases is under appeal. An application to foreclose on a couple who had not made payments on their mortgage since last August was made and dismissed by the court. The couple had declared bankruptcy last December, and the court in its judgment ruled that there was no basis upon which the action could proceed against them. Incidentally, there was considerable equity in the house despite the fact that the couple had declared bankruptcy.
Then in Saskatoon Justice J. H. Maher ruled that a Saskatoon resident must make mortgage payments at an increased interest rate despite pleas of financial hardship. Mr. Justice Maher said that the 17.5 per cent mortgage renewal offered was in line with prevailing rates. The old mortgage rate had been 11 per cent, so there was a substantial increase in the monthly payments. The result after some two months and two tests is that no one knows where we are going.
CMHC is concerned about insured loan arrears and claims on the mortgage insurance fund. The reason for this is that in the event of a claim under the mortgage loan insurance policy the corporation, under existing legislation, can only pay interest at the full mortgage rate for 12 months from the date interest is due, or accrued and unpaid, and mortgage interest less 2 per cent for a further six months. In other words, there is a total 18-month limitation on the liability of the corporation. As a result, CMHC communicated with its officers in the province of Saskatchewan that for any new loan commitment an NHA undertaking to insure will be conditional on the Saskatchewan home owners protection act having no effect whatever in the event of a claim under the insurance settlement provisions of the National Housing Act.
It is quite apparent that the influence of provinces on housing is considerable. 1 will go a step further and say that their effect has been detrimental to the interests of Canadian citizens. At the present time six of the ten provinces have rent control legislation. I understand why rent control legislation is in force and why there is pressure to maintain rent control legislation.
Nevertheless, let us look at the facts. At the moment in British Columbia there is a 10 per cent limit on rent increases; in Ontario, the figure is 6 per cent; in Nova Scotia, 4 per cent;

February 25, 1982
Housing
in Prince Edward Island it varies between 4 per cent and 8 per cent. We have rent controls in Saskatchewan, and in all probability Manitoba, where there was a recent change in government, will also impose some form of rent control. The estimated gap between rents required to render rental construction viable and market rents is now between $120 and $200 per month per unit. As a result we have a very tight rental market at the present time. It has been suggested that if there is not some adjustment in rents in the very near future to make rental construction viable, the situation will become even more serious; in fact, somewhat disastrous.
The alternative is for governments-and I mean both federal and provincial governments-to enter into permanent and costly long-term support for the construction of rental housing, depending upon degree. Of course, we can bandy around various figures, but there is no doubt that we are talking about many billions of dollars.
It is unfortunate that some provinces, particularly the province of Quebec, do not take advantage of the programs which are presently available. I listened to the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) screaming earlier this afternoon. I think he should direct his attention to the provincial government in Quebec City which, because of its hatred of the federal system and its desire to dissociate itself in any form from the federal government, has not only failed to recognize the part the federal government has played but has refused to participate in programs which will be of direct assistance to the residents of that province.
I have looked at some figures concerning the assisted rental program. As I have put on the record previously, the program cost the federal treasury through CMHC some $186 million. Because some 80 per cent of that housing was in the province of Quebec, one can roughly calculate so far an involvement of about $150 million in rental housing in that province under ARP. That is not all by any means. That is only the up front moneys. The amount which is charged for the insurance of the mortgage under this program is 1 per cent and it has been estimated that the rate should be in the order of 8 per cent. This is also an indirect subsidy. I mention these figures because too often these days the government of the province of Quebec is choosing to ignore the part the federal government has played in trying to assist the citizens of Quebec.
I was particularly angry a couple of nights ago when a member of the Pequiste government said on the radio that the federal government is cutting the funds that were going into that province. I suspect that we are sometimes a little reluctant to talk about the moneys that go to the province of Quebec, but I want to put on the record that when that Pequiste member said the amount was being cut by some $600 million,
I have no idea how he arrived at his figures but I suggest that he forgot that during this fiscal year-and I say during the fiscal year, not over the term of the whole year-the program of equalization of which the province of Quebec is a major participant saw the total funds from the federal treasury
increased from $1.7 billion to $2.1 billion. Last spring the Pequiste government could have included in its budget the total of $1.7 billion. However, it is getting an additional $400 million this year. That is not talked about.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) when talking about the Canada Assistance Plan mentioned the amount of the increase this year. Extrapolating the figures for the province of Quebec, although the precise totals are not yet ready, one can see that the province has received something in the order of $150 million more in fiscal year, 1981-1982, ending March 31. Just in those two programs alone there is $550 million of extra moneys which the province of Quebec could not have counted upon last spring.
Let us look at federal programs that have been offered to all provinces, of which the majority of provinces make use and which the province of Quebec chooses to ignore. First, the rural and native housing program. The new housing component is cost shared. Quebec refuses to sign the agreement. The result is that no affordable housing is being built under the rural and native housing program. Quebec is prepared to borrow money from the federal treasury. In fact, that province will take all the money it can get but it will not sign ownership agreements. I suppose one can acknowledge that is the province's right, but I want everyone to realize that this lack of cooperation between the government of the province of Quebec and the federal government is very costly to the citizens of Quebec.
Second is the non-profit and co-operative housing. This program does not reach the lower income band, again because of lack of Quebec participation. The federal government provides subsidies. Quebec could provide an equivalent subsidy, but it chooses not to. Once again the opportunity is not used. Therefore, we have this continuing conflict between the two levels of government. I suppose one can say that is its provincial right. I will accept that, but I do not want that same government that chooses not to co-operate to return and complain. The opportunity is there. It has made no alternative suggestions except to turn over the funding.
When we challenge the government of the province of Quebec as to whether it will take the funding, it expresses some reluctance. The reason is obvious. If the government of the province of Quebec chooses to take tax points instead of cash from the federal treasury, it will lose several hundred million dollars. The reason is very simple. The tax base in the province of Quebec is steadily declining and deteriorating as people have moved out. For example, retired people with high incomes have decided to move elsewhere to get the benefit of lower tax rates. No longer does the Quebec government have the choice that it used to talk about for years of taking its own tax points. I challenge my provincial colleagues in Quebec and I challenge the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. LaSalle) to acknowledge the fact that the province of Quebec has had quite a good deal from the federal government. Furthermore, not only has it had a good deal, but it had been offered a lot better deal which it turned down.
February 25, 1982

In the motion such as the one I have proposed this afternoon for the production of documents-and I have proposed several in this House-the intent on my part is to underline that a great many more documents not marked secret or confidential should be in the public domain. They should be accessible not just to members of Parliament but to the public at large.
We are hearing a lot of discussion these days about the freedom of information bill. I am not particularly interested in this bill myself. I do not even know what we are expecting to produce that we are not presently getting. What I am talking about are documents that are in no sense secret documents, or confidential documents, but documents which are necessary, in my opinion, so that the public can better understand what the federal government is doing in its various programs and what agreements the federal government is making with the provincial governments.
Just last week I spoke of the Canada Assistance Plan. Its guidelines were established by the federal government but they were not published. I suggest that the federal government should sincerely look at opening up a public perusal of all of these guidelines and communications between the federal and provincial governments, and in cases where the provincial government refuses to make such documents public, to acknowledge that fact and to tell the public that it is not the federal government but the provincial government that is refusing to disclose. There may be good reasons and they can be made public, but the purpose of this motion is to underline the fact that too many documents at the present time that have absolutely no reason whatever for being kept under wraps should be made available upon demand through Members of Parliament to the public at large.
That is the reason I have brought forward this motion for discussion today. Also, it enables me to discuss once again in some measure the problem of division of jurisdiction between the two levels of government, the provincial government which is essentially responsible for the physical construction aspects and the federal government which tends to do its part through its fiscal powers.

subtopic: COMMUNICATIONS BETWEEN GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCEOF SASKATCHEWAN CONCERNING RESIDENTIAL MORTGAGES AND HOME FORECLOSURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion presented to the House by the hon. member for Vau-dreuil (Mr. Herbert) gives us the opportunity to consider the role of Canada Mortage and Housing Corporation in relation to two very important matters, matters of great concern to the people of Canada today, namely, the residential mortgage and the interest rate thereon, and the number of home foreclosures occurring across this country arising from the inability of home owners to meet the interest rates being imposed upon them.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we have to consider a very basic fact and principle of Canadian life: family security is often related to the ability of that family to provide adequate housing. There are other essentials of life, of course, including food, clothing and education. However, if a family unit cannot properly house itself, then it is bound to experience difficulties.
Housing
Home ownership has always been the dream of Canadians. That was my party's view when we proposed a program to assist Canadians in providing for home ownership for their families. That program involved mortgage interest and property tax deductibility for home owners. Mr. Speaker, the government of today opposed that program when it was presented in this House and as a result the principle of assistance to home owners was defeated. We are paying the price for that opposition today because there are thousands of Canadians across the country faced with the problem of extraordinarily high levels of mortgage interest.
Today the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) revels in the fact that mortgage interest rates have declined over the past few months, although they are still at a level of 18 per cent or 19 per cent. There are many Canadians who, because of the kind of homes they have or must purchase, are not able to negotiate a mortgage at that rate and are forced to pay much higher rates.
Now, Mr. Speaker, relating that situation to the problem of foreclosure-the ultimate sanction against a home owner unable to meet mortgage payments-we have to consider not only the immediate and practical consequences, but the social consequences which flow from the loss of a home. It is not only demeaning to the family, but it creates greater problems which must be resolved by government through social service programs. The family placed on the street without funds must apply to a municipal or provincial welfare agency to obtain housing, and that quite often involves public expense. This means it is possible to make a case for very substantial government involvement in the residential mortgage field by way of direct and indirect assistance. As I indicated, our party attempted to do that, but having failed in that endeavour we must now look at what kind of assistance we can provide in today's circumstances.
This debate is very timely, Mr. Speaker, because Bill C-89 purports to deal with, in part, the housing problem and the problem of those unable to meet their mortgage payments. The bill, Mr. Speaker, is a paltry measure when compared with the plight home owners find themselves in. Even so, Mr. Speaker, the minister responsible for housing rose in the House today to direct that debate be halted on this measure. He wants to remove from parliamentarians the opportunity to address the difficulties which arise because of high mortgage interest rates. He wants to stop discussions which might produce more effective and generous measures to assist home owners. That is not only a blow to the parliamentary system, it is a tremendous blow to those Canadians who look to the federal government for assistance with this very special problem.
Now, why do they have that problem, Mr. Speaker? It is because over the last ten years the government has spent the public's money in a wasteful manner, which has led to a situation where the internal and external value of our dollar has dropped. As a result, in order to provide any return to investors, interest rates have increased so substantially that they affect the ability of Canadians to provide themselves with housing.

February 25, 1982
Housing
There is more to the case to be made for governmental assistance to home owners. There are reports in the press every day that the housing construction industry has slumped to the point where it is becoming a national problem. Many jobs have been lost in the residential construction sector. Contractors across the country are going bankrupt. Demand for homes has decreased to the point where there is very little construction going on. To the extent there is a need for housing and there are people who can afford to purchase at today's rates, we have a situation where the builders simply cannot get an appropriate return for their efforts. As a result, they withdraw from the housing construction field. So not only do we have a problem of people losing their homes due to high interest rates; it also has a very dramatic effect on the entire construction industry, particularly the home construction sector.
What does the minister responsible for housing propose? In regard to the resulting unemployment, he proposes a very minor program which will provide $7,500 for rental unit construction. He proposes assistance only for those in absolute dire straits, which assistance to that very limited group will only help them over a very short period of time and only on the basis of a loan or recoverable assistance. Mr. Speaker, the situation calls for much more dramatic action. It requires very special aid. Canadians who can renegotiate a mortgage in the $50,000 range-not a great deal when you consider that hardly anywhere can you buy a home for less than $70,000- will find their monthly payments increasing by almost $300 a month. Yet their salaries have not increased at the same rate and they do not have the ability to meet the increase.
What happens then, Mr. Speaker? That brings us to the issue of foreclosure. What, in specific terms, is foreclosure? Well, the home owner who can no longer carry his mortgage payments is faced with a legal process whereby the family home is sold to recover the debt represented by the mortgage. In very few cases is there anything left over for the home owner. Foreclosure is usually triggered by a situation where the mortgage debt is at least as great as, or greater than, the value of the home. So the result is that the home owner, after paying the mortgage and municipal taxes for years and after having made improvements to the home, is left with absolutely nothing. We must, therefore, recognize that foreclosure is one of the most cruel forms of legal action that can be taken. In 90 per cent, if not all, of these cases, the home owner is left with nothing. In addition, he has to seek housing in some other area which may well cost just as much in terms of total monthly expenses.
In most cases the housing, which is the subject of foreclosure action, is only adequate for the needs of the family involved. They will face the same problem that existed before the foreclosure action occurred; that is, the provision of adequate housing, and it will face the same mortgage payments which, as has already been established, it could not meet before. My point is that this becomes a problem for government; it becomes a social welfare problem, and at that point, the government does step in.
What I am asking, and what I hope all hon. members will ask, is that the government take preventive action by providing assistance which will be operative before the home owners reach the point where they lose their homes through foreclosure action. If we are going to provide assistance, let us not wait until the damage is done and the homes are lost. Let us provide assistance at the time when the home owners can do something to maintain themselves and their families in their homes.
That kind of assistance has to be much greater and broader than the assistance the minister responsible for housing proposes in the bill now before the House. That is why hon. members in this party and on this side of the House have urged the minister, time and time again, to broaden the base of the assistance and to make it more substantial. That is why we would not be doing our duty to our constituents and to Canadians in general, if we did not stand up in this House at every opportunity and indicate to the minister that his program is not sufficient, that it will not solve the problem, and that greater action is required.
There certainly are many who say that interest rates ought not to be subsidized, as that just puts off a resolution to the problem. We have heard from the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), time and time again, that there must be a longterm solution to the problem, that we have to suffer through this difficult period so that the economy will recover and interest rates will decrease later on in the normal course of economic events.
However, we are playing with people's lives. We are speaking about Canadians, about individuals who live in homes, who want to maintain their families and who want to look forward to the future with some hope and some confidence. It is not just an economic matter, a matter of simply adding up figures and balancing payments in books, and so on. We are dealing with people, and we have to recognize that. That is why drastic situations require drastic action.
Therefore, I would say to anyone who dares to suggest that the situation is not so difficult or that we do not need to take this very specific kind of action, that person should cross the country and speak to the people who are in the situation of not being able to meet the mortgage payments being demanded of them. Talk to them and consider their problems. I am sure that any Member of Parliament or any Canadian who did that would change his or her mind concerning the matter of assistance for those home owners who find they cannot meet the financial obligations imposed upon them.
The instrument through which we have to effect housing policies nationally is the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. That is why it is so important that this motion be considered by hon. members of the House. It points the finger at Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and really, in effect, asks the question, "What is going on with that government agency in relation to residential mortgages and foreclosures?"
As 1 look at the newspapers of my own city of Halifax, as well as those of Ottawa, Montreal and Toronto, I note that
February 25, 1982

most of the foreclosure actions in Canada are instituted by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. There is a reason for that. It is that the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation tends to overlend on homes; that is to say, the amount of money it provides in mortgage funds is sometimes almost as great as the market value of the homes. In many cases, it is even greater. The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation has created a situation in which a home owner does not have any real equity in his property. He has simply made payments by way of rent over a period of years, and even though he thought he was in an ownership position, in actual fact he is merely a renter because Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation has simply used his down payment, perhaps his effort in improving the house, and the money he has expended for public utilities and other services necessary, to maintain that home over the years. As a result, after as many as five or ten years, that home owner is left with nothing.
The point I am trying to make is simply that Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation creates situations by its policies which it then seeks to remedy by drastic legal action. The government should simply admit that the whole purpose of the program was to provide subsidized housing to the individual. In other words, to those who say that we ought not to provide subsidization for home ownership in Canada, I say we are already doing it, and we have been doing it for years. We have tried to mask it, refer to it by another name and pretend it is not subsidization.
We have tried to pretend, for example, with the Assisted Home Ownership Program, AHOP, that there is an actual sale of a house for the value of that house. That is not true at all. There have been no real sales. That is why many AHOP owners find that they lose their subsidy, Five years down the road, when they cannot meet current interest rates and are simply not able to carry on.
The point is that the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation created that situation. The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation ought not to be allowed to simply withdraw and say it is dealing with these matters as business transactions, and if one cannot make one's payment, it will take foreclosure proceedings. This means that the owner will lose the home on which he has been paying for the past five years or more.
Some people want to deny assistance to home owners in Canada because they characterize home owners as rich people who do not require assistance, as the Minister of Finance did, in the 1980 election campaign when he was an hon. member of the opposition. The minister said that home owners were rich people who did not require assistance, and that government resources should be used in other ways to provide help to persons who rent their housing facilities, and to provide assistance to senior citizens, but not to provide assistance to rich home owners in Canada. That was simply not true. It was a myth, which the present Minister of Finance created; that there was this group of rich home owners in Canada who did not require assistance. We are seeing the realities of the situation today. We are seeing home owners who cannot
Housing
maintain their mortgage payments and, as I have indicated, the result is foreclosure. They are on the street, and they become public charges. One simply spends the same dollar bills through the social assistance program instead of through an adequate housing program.
The whole point of my remarks is simply that one cannot escape problems by pretending to resolve them. One cannot nationalize poverty. One must deal with the economic facts as they exist across Canada. One of the economic facts of today is that home owners, in so many cases, cannot afford higher rates of interest. They cannot come up with the dollars they need to make the monthly payments required of them. If they are not given appropriate and proper assistance, the whole situation will simply collapse. Foreclosure will result, and these people will be out on the street. Then the government will have to deal with that social problem at the municipal, provincial and federal levels.
I hope the important message of my remarks and the motion which the hon. member has brought before the House is understood. Let us get the facts. Let us find out what is happening with mortgage interest rates. Let us find out what is happening with foreclosure actions. Let us find out what the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation is doing. Let us assess the situation in light of those facts. If we make a fair assessment, I think we will very quickly come to the conclusion that very definite action must be taken by government, and that the action which has been taken by the minister responsible for housing, represented by the bill now before the House, is simply inadequate. It will not solve the problem. In fact, it may even exacerbate it because it will simply keep alive, for just a few months or a few years, those people who will have to face the realities of their situation somewhere down the road. All we are doing is patching the problem. This is not even band-aid treatment. We are not dealing with the issue, we are just avoiding it.
Therefore, I support the hon. member in attempting to obtain the kind of information which will allow for a fair and proper assessment of the housing situation in Canada, of the role of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and of the dire effects of foreclosure actions, because if we get those facts examined and assess them, I think we will then conclude that drastic measures are required. I think we will then be able to join together and devise those measures which will relieve the situation and resolve the problem for the benefit of all Canadians.
